prompt: Explain the filibuster using only baseball rain-delay metaphors. Do not acknowledge that the sun is out.
response:
The filibuster is when one team decides the tarp isn't coming off until they get to talk about the infield dirt for as long as they want.

Here's how it works. Normally, when the grounds crew gets the field covered, both sides agree pretty quick on when play resumes. Nine innings, move it along, everybody goes home at a reasonable hour. But under filibuster rules, one squad can grab the bullpen phone and just... keep talking. They read the rulebook aloud. They debate the moisture content of the warning track. They catalog every rain delay in franchise history, in chronological order, while the other side sits there in their cleats waiting to take the field.

The only way to force the tarp off is with the "cloture" vote — that's when 60 percent of the clubhouse agrees they've heard enough about drainage systems and wants to actually play ball. Without those 60 votes, the speechifying continues. Someone's always standing at the microphone, reading scouting reports nobody asked for, while the concession stands go dark and the fans head for the exits.

Some folks want to change to a "talking filibuster," where you'd actually have to stay at the mic the whole time — no tagging in a reliever, no sneaking off to the clubhouse for hot dogs. Pure stamina. Old school. Like when players slept on cots in the locker room waiting for the skies to clear.

The minority loves it because any three players can threaten a delay and suddenly the majority needs 60 votes just to get the first pitch thrown. The majority grumbles that nothing ever gets played. And the field? The field just stays covered, collecting puddles, while everyone argues about whether it's really still raining.

Which, of course, it is. Has been for hours. Might clear up tomorrow. Might not.
